config.title: Build deep equality function

intro.title: Build deep equality function
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a function that checks if two values are deeply equal, meaning it compares their contents thoroughly, even for nested objects and arrays. You will learn how to handle different data types like primitives, arrays, and objects using recursion and iteration. The main technologies involved are JavaScript functions, conditional statements, loops, and the typeof operator. This exercise will help you understand how to compare complex data structures accurately, a common task in programming.
intro.usecase: Deep equality checks are essential when comparing complex data structures in real applications. For example, when building a dashboard that monitors real-time stock prices, you need to compare previous and current market data objects to detect meaningful changes before updating charts. In form validation systems, deep equality helps determine if user-edited profile data differs from the original before enabling save buttons. React and Vue applications use deep equality internally to optimize re-renders by comparing previous and current props/state objects efficiently.

objectives: Implement a function that compares primitive values for equality
Construct logic to handle null and undefined values in equality checks
Apply recursion to compare nested objects and arrays
Manipulate iteration to traverse object keys and array elements
Configure type checking to distinguish between arrays and objects
Integrate edge case handling for different data types
Control the comparison flow with early returns for performance

steps.title: Create the deepEqual function skeleton
steps.instruction: Create a function named deepEqual that takes two parameters (a and b) and returns a boolean value. You can use either a function declaration or arrow function syntax.
steps.hint: Start by writing 'function deepEqual(a, b)' or 'const deepEqual = (a, b) =>', then add curly braces and return a boolean (like true or false for now).
steps.expectedOutcome: A function named deepEqual is defined with two parameters and returns a boolean value.
successCriteria: The code contains a function named deepEqual with parameters a and b that returns a boolean value.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure your function is named exactly 'deepEqual', takes two parameters (a and b), and returns a boolean value (like true or false).
steps.feedbackWrong: Create a function named deepEqual that accepts two parameters and returns a boolean value. Check your syntax and make sure you're using the correct function name.

steps.title: Add basic type checking for primitive values
steps.instruction: Inside your deepEqual function, add a check that returns true if a and b are strictly equal (a === b).
steps.hint: Use the strict equality operator (===) to compare a and b directly. If they are equal, return true.
steps.expectedOutcome: The function will immediately return true when a and b are strictly equal primitive values.
successCriteria: The deepEqual function contains an if statement that checks a === b and returns true if they are equal.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're using strict equality (===) and returning true when the values match.
steps.feedbackWrong: The function should check if a and b are strictly equal using === and return true when they match.

steps.title: Check if both values are objects and not null
steps.instruction: Inside your deepEqual function, add a condition to check if both a and b are objects (using typeof) and neither is null.
steps.hint: Use typeof to check if both values are 'object', then add an additional check that they are not null.
steps.expectedOutcome: Your deepEqual function will now have a condition that checks if both inputs are objects and not null.
successCriteria: The condition uses typeof to check for 'object' type and includes a null check for both a and b.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure to check both a and b are objects AND not null. Review the typeof operator and null comparison.
steps.feedbackWrong: The condition is missing or incorrect. Remember to use typeof a === 'object' && typeof b === 'object' && a !== null && b !== null.

steps.title: Handle null or non-object cases
steps.instruction: Inside your deepEqual function, add an early return that checks if either value is null or not an object, and returns false in those cases.
steps.hint: You can use the typeof operator and a strict equality check for null. Remember we already handled primitive equality in step 2.
steps.expectedOutcome: The function should now return false immediately when either a or b is null or not an object, before proceeding to deeper object comparison.
successCriteria: The deepEqual function includes an early return that checks both a and b for null or non-object types and returns false when either condition is met.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure to check both parameters (a and b) for null and non-object types. Both checks should return false if either condition is true.
steps.feedbackWrong: The function should handle null and non-object cases by returning false before attempting deeper comparison. Check both parameters using typeof and strict equality for null.

steps.title: Get keys from both objects
steps.instruction: Inside your deepEqual function, after the constructor check, create two variables: keysA and keysB. Use Object.keys() on both input objects to get their property names.
steps.hint: You can assign the result of Object.keys(a) to keysA, and Object.keys(b) to keysB.
steps.expectedOutcome: You will have two variables (keysA and keysB) that hold arrays of property names from each object.
successCriteria: The deepEqual function contains variables keysA and keysB assigned with Object.keys(a) and Object.keys(b).
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're using Object.keys() on both 'a' and 'b' to create keysA and keysB.
steps.feedbackWrong: create two variables (keysA and keysB) using Object.keys() on the input objects.

steps.title: Compare number of keys
steps.instruction: Inside your deepEqual function, after getting the keys arrays, check if their lengths are different. If they are, return false.
steps.hint: You can compare the lengths of keysA and keysB using the strict inequality operator (!==).
steps.expectedOutcome: The function will now return false early when objects have different numbers of keys, improving efficiency.
successCriteria: The deepEqual function includes a check comparing keysA.length and keysB.length, returning false if they differ.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're comparing the lengths of keysA and keysB and returning false if they're different.
steps.feedbackWrong: Try again. You need to add a check inside deepEqual that compares the lengths of the keys arrays and returns false if they're not equal.

steps.title: Iterate through keys for comparison
steps.instruction: Inside your deepEqual function, create a for...of loop to iterate through the keysA array.
steps.hint: Use the syntax 'for (const key of keysA) { }' to loop through each key in the array.
steps.expectedOutcome: The function will have a for...of loop that iterates through the keysA array.
successCriteria: A for...of loop is created inside the deepEqual function that iterates through the keysA array.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're using a for...of loop to iterate through the keysA array.
steps.feedbackWrong: Try again. You need to create a for...of loop inside the deepEqual function to iterate through the keysA array.

steps.title: Check if key exists in both objects
steps.instruction: Inside the for...of loop, check if the current key exists in object 'b' using the hasOwnProperty method. If it doesn't exist, return false.
steps.hint: Use b.hasOwnProperty(key) to check if the key exists in the second object. Remember to return false immediately if the check fails.
steps.expectedOutcome: The function will now check that each key from object 'a' also exists in object 'b' before proceeding to value comparison.
successCriteria: The for...of loop includes a check using b.hasOwnProperty(key) that returns false when the key is missing from object 'b'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're using hasOwnProperty on object 'b' and returning false when the key doesn't exist.
steps.feedbackWrong: The key existence check is missing or incorrect. Inside the loop, use b.hasOwnProperty(key) to verify the key exists in both objects, returning false if it doesn't.

steps.title: Add recursive call for nested objects
steps.instruction: Inside the loop, call deepEqual recursively on a[key] and b[key], returning false if the recursive call returns false.
steps.hint: Use the deepEqual function itself to compare the values of each key. If the recursive call returns false, you should return false from the current function.
steps.expectedOutcome: The deepEqual function will now recursively compare nested objects when it encounters them during iteration.
successCriteria: The loop includes a recursive call to deepEqual for comparing a[key] and b[key], and returns false when the recursive call returns false.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure to return false when the recursive call returns false.
steps.feedbackWrong: The recursive call is missing or not properly implemented. Check if you're calling deepEqual with a[key] and b[key] and handling the return value correctly.

steps.title: Return true after all checks pass
steps.instruction: After the for...in loop completes (meaning all keys have been successfully compared), add a return true statement at the end of your deepEqual function.
steps.hint: Place the return true statement after the closing brace of your for...in loop, but before the closing brace of the function.
steps.expectedOutcome: The deepEqual function will now correctly return true when all properties match between two objects.
successCriteria: The function ends with a return true statement after the loop.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you've added a return true statement at the end of the function, after the loop completes.
steps.feedbackWrong: The function needs to return true when all checks pass. Add a return true statement after the for...in loop.

steps.title: Test the deepEqual function
steps.instruction: Add test cases after your deepEqual function to verify it works correctly with different inputs.
steps.hint: Call deepEqual with various test values and log the results using console.log.
steps.expectedOutcome: You should see console output showing true/false results from your deepEqual tests.
successCriteria: Test cases are added that call deepEqual with at least two different input pairs and log the results.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You added some test cases, but try to include a few more different inputs to thoroughly test the function.
steps.feedbackWrong: No test cases were added. Add at least two calls to deepEqual with different inputs and log the results.
